Rescue workers and military personnel have been working around the clock since Wednesday’s disaster

  • ‘The flood took everything I have’: survivors grieve for relatives and homes swept away in Nepal

  • Chinese rescuers find ‘nothing but ruins’ at border crossing as Nepal seeks help to ID and store the dead

The Guardian’s south Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis-Petersen and journalist Gaurav Pokharel report from the Nepalese town of Bidur, where rescue efforts are being coordinated. They spoke to survivors mourning loved ones and confronting the loss of their homes and livelihoods after devastating floods swept through their communities.

Among those caught in the floods was Sangke Dolma Tamang, who described the moment she watched her husband being swept away and returned to find her home and village destroyed:

Sangke Dolma Tamang, 61, had been cheerily cooking snacks in her village of Mailung in the Rasuwa district when the floods came without warning. The whole family ran uphill for safety, but as she grabbed for her husband, he slipped from her grip and was washed into the dark, fast-moving waters.

“Others tried to pull him to safety, but the flood swept him away,” she said, tears rolling down her weathered cheeks. There was, she said, nothing left of her village now. She had spent a night sheltering on higher ground, until an army helicopter arrived and brought to her safety at the barracks. Her son too was missing since the disaster, and she waited anxiously for any news.

items.title: La tragédie au Népal met en garde contre un danger croissant : 15 millions de personnes vivent sous la menace des lacs glaciaires
items.content_html:
La inondation monstrueuse du Tibet et du Népal, qui a causé des centaines de morts et des milliers de personnes disparues, a rendu le risque de vivre en montagne des chaînes de montagnes avec des glaciers, puisque tout indique qu'une de ces masses de glace s'est effondrée et a déclenché la tragédie. Le phénomène est connu sous le nom de GLOF (Glacier Lake Outburst Flood), une crue soudaine provoquée par le débordement d'un lac glaciaire. Le le changement climatique et son augmentation des températures sont à l'origine de ces événements : les inondations ont été multipliées par six au siècle dernier. Les grandes chaînes de montagnes comme l'Himalaya, les Andes ou les Alpes concentrent les endroits où se produisent le plus ce type d'inondations, auxquelles sont exposées 15 millions de personnes dans le monde, dont la moitié au Pérou, en Inde, en Chine et au Pakistan. Surveiller les glaciers et les lagons n'est pas facile, surtout dans les pays en développement, mais cela sauve des vies : l'année dernière, une ville de Suisse a été évacuée deux jours avant l'effondrement d'un autre glacier.

As thousands of residents in Spokane, Washington, begin to grapple with a long recovery after a destructive set of blazes that consumed hundreds of homes in the state’s second most populated city this month, victims of the Los Angeles firestorm broke a grim record – they have faced the longest delay in modern history for federal aid.

Nearly 600 days since a historic firestorm roared into communities across Los Angeles, reducing more than 16,000 structures to ash and toxic debris, the Trump administration has failed to appropriate more than $15bn in long-term recovery funds that are crucial to rebuilding. But the central challenge is already clear: this cannot be treated solely as an immediate humanitarian emergency. What happens to these communities in the years ahead depends heavily on what we do now.
